Fix an integer $N\ge1$, put $h=1/N$, and let $x_j=jh$ for $j=0,\ldots,N$. The cells are $K_j=[x_{j-1},x_j]$. For $g_0,g_1\in\mathbb R$, let $S_h(g_0,g_1)$ be the finite-dimensional space of continuous functions on $[0,1]$ that are affine on each cell and have endpoint values $g_0,g_1$. Write $V_h=S_h(0,0)$ for the homogeneous test and trial space. “P1” means polynomial degree at most one on each interval.

Let $\epsilon>0$, $b\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}$, and $f\in C([0,1])$. The stationary boundary-value problem is to find $u\in C^2([0,1])$ such that $-\epsilon u''+b u'=f$ on $(0,1)$, with prescribed endpoint values $u(0)=g_0$ and $u(1)=g_1$. Its dimensionless cell Péclet number is $\mathrm{Pe}=|b|h/(2\epsilon)>0$. The stability theorem on this page uses the homogeneous branch $g_0=g_1=0$; the general endpoint notation also permits the boundary-layer example.

derivations.claim: Fix a cell $K=[a,b]$ of length $h_K$, and let $s_K=(u(b)-u(a))/h_K$ be the slope of $I_hu$ on $K$. By the fundamental theorem of calculus, $s_K=h_K^{-1}\int_a^b u'(t)\,dt$. For every $x\in K$, the same theorem gives $|u'(x)-u'(t)|\le h_K\|u''\|_\infty$, so averaging in $t$ yields $|(u-I_hu)'(x)|=|u'(x)-s_K|\le h_K\|u''\|_\infty$.

Since $(u-I_hu)(a)=0$, integrating the derivative bound from step 1.1 over $[a,x]$ gives $|u(x)-I_hu(x)|\le h_K^2\|u''\|_\infty$ for every $x\in K$. Therefore $\|u-I_hu\|_{L^2(K)}^2\le h_K^5\|u''\|_\infty^2$.

The cell interiors are disjoint, their lengths sum to $1$, and $h_K\le h$, so $\sum_Kh_K^5\le h^4\sum_Kh_K=h^4$. Summing step 2.1 over the cells and taking nonnegative square roots proves the estimate.

Fix an integer $d\ge2$. The underlying coordinate index set of $\mathbb R^d$
is $I_d=\{0,\ldots,d-1\}$. In this definition the conventional labels
$1\le i\le d$ are relabeled by $i\mapsto i-1$: write
$\widehat x_i:=\widehat x(i-1)$, and let $e_i\in\mathbb R^d$ be the function
on $I_d$ with $e_i(i-1)=1$ and $e_i(k)=0$ for $k\ne i-1$.
The vertex and barycentric labels $0,\ldots,d$ are distinct from these
underlying coordinate indices. The **reference open simplex** is
$$\widehat S_d:=\{\widehat x\in\mathbb R^d:\widehat x_i>0\ (1\le i\le d),\ \sum_{i=1}^d\widehat x_i<1\},$$
with closure $\overline{\widehat S_d}=\operatorname{conv}\{0,e_1,\ldots,e_d\}$.

A **matching affine simplicial mesh** of a bounded polyhedral open set
$\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ is a finite set $\mathcal T$ of closed,
nondegenerate $d$-simplices such that their union is $\overline\Omega$,
their interiors are pairwise disjoint, $\Omega$ is the interior of their
union, and the intersection of two distinct cells is either empty or a
whole face of each. Thus no lower-dimensional crack is omitted from
$\Omega$ while its surrounding cells are retained. Every interior facet is
incident to exactly two cells and every boundary facet to one. The faces of
a cell are the convex hulls of its vertex subsets. A facet means a face of
dimension $d-1$.

For each cell $K\in\mathcal T$, an affine bijection
$$F_K:\overline{\widehat S_d}\to K,\qquad F_K(\widehat x)=b_K+A_K\widehat x,$$
with invertible $A_K\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ is a **reference map**.
Choose the vertex order so $\det A_K>0$; this is the orientation convention
used for Piola formulas. Write $h_K:=\operatorname{diam}(K)$ and let
$\rho_K$ be the radius of the largest Euclidean ball contained in $K$.
A family $\{\mathcal T_h\}_{h\in H}$ is **shape regular** if there is a
finite $\sigma$ such that $h_K/\rho_K\le\sigma$ for every
$h\in H$ and $K\in\mathcal T_h$. This universal condition is vacuous for
an empty family.
This definition uses radius; references using the diameter of the inscribed
ball differ by a factor of two.

An affine image of the reference square is a parallelogram. A general
quadrilateral requires a nonaffine map and is outside this affine definition;
curved-cell approximation is not included here.

Fix $d\ge2$ and a bounded connected polyhedral open set $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$. For each mesh parameter $h$, let $\mathcal T_h$ be a finite matching shape-regular affine simplicial mesh in the sense of [[def-matching-affine-simplicial-meshes]], and put $h=\max_{K\in\mathcal T_h}h_K$. Let $V_h$ be the space of continuous functions on $\overline\Omega$ that are affine on every cell and vanish on $\partial\Omega$.

Let $\epsilon>0$, $b\in C^1(\overline\Omega;\mathbb R^d)$, $c\in C(\overline\Omega)$, and $f\in C(\overline\Omega)$. Define $B:=\|b\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)}$ and $C:=\|c\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)}$. Assume a fixed $\omega>0$ satisfies $c-\frac12\nabla\cdot b\ge\omega$ on $\Omega$. The boundary condition for this branch is $u=0$ on the whole boundary, including the inflow part $\{x\in\partial\Omega:b(x)\cdot n(x)<0\}$. A classical exact solution is a function $u\in C^2(\overline\Omega)$ satisfying $-\epsilon\Delta u+b\cdot\nabla u+cu=f$ in $\Omega$ and this boundary condition.

derivations.claim: Fix a cell $K$ and a vertex $a_0$. Taylor's formula along the segment from $a_0$ to $x\in K$ gives $u(x)=p_K(x)+r_K(x)$ with $p_K(x)=u(a_0)+\nabla u(a_0)\cdot(x-a_0)$, $|r_K(x)|\le\frac12h_K^2\|D^2u\|_{L^\infty(K)}$, and $|\nabla r_K(x)|\le h_K\|D^2u\|_{L^\infty(K)}$.

The nodal interpolant reproduces $p_K$, so $u-I_Ku=r_K-\sum_i r_K(a_i)\lambda_i$. On $K$, $0\le\lambda_i\le1$ and $\sum_i\lambda_i=1$. The altitude from any vertex to its opposite facet is at least $\rho_K$, hence $|\nabla\lambda_i|\le\rho_K^{-1}\le\sigma h_K^{-1}$ by [F1]. Substitution of the bounds in step 1.1 gives $|u-I_Ku|\le C(d)h_K^2\|D^2u\|_{L^\infty(K)}$ and $|\nabla(u-I_Ku)|\le C(d,\sigma)h_K\|D^2u\|_{L^\infty(K)}$.

Squaring the two pointwise bounds, integrating on each cell, summing over the finite mesh, using $h_K\le h$ and $\sum_K|K|=|\Omega|$, and taking square roots proves both global estimates with $M_2=|\Omega|^{1/2}\|D^2u\|_\infty$.

On a shared interior facet, the affine traces from its two incident cells agree at all facet vertices, so they agree everywhere on that facet; thus the cell interpolants assemble to a continuous $I_hu$. If $u$ vanishes on a boundary facet, all its vertices there have zero nodal values, so the affine trace also vanishes there. This proves both global conformity and the boundary claim.

Let $X_c$ and $X_f$ be finite-dimensional real vector spaces and set $X=X_c\oplus X_f$; elements are written $(u_c,u_f)$, with $u_c$ the resolved component and $u_f$ the unresolved component. For a real vector space $Y$, let $Y^*$ be its space of real linear functionals. Let $A_{cc}:X_c\to X_c^*$, $A_{cf}:X_f\to X_c^*$, $A_{fc}:X_c\to X_f^*$, and $A_{ff}:X_f\to X_f^*$ be linear maps, with $A_{ff}$ invertible, and let $F_c\in X_c^*$ and $F_f\in X_f^*$. The linear equation on $X$ has block form
$$\begin{pmatrix}A_{cc}&A_{cf}\\A_{fc}&A_{ff}\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}u_c\\u_f\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}F_c\\F_f\end{pmatrix}.$$
The fine residual for a resolved vector $v_c$ is $r_f(v_c):=F_f-A_{fc}v_c$. Exact elimination gives $u_f=A_{ff}^{-1}r_f(u_c)$ and the Schur equation
$$\left(A_{cc}-A_{cf}A_{ff}^{-1}A_{fc}\right)u_c=F_c-A_{cf}A_{ff}^{-1}F_f.$$

A **residual closure** selects a linear map $T:X_f^*\to X_f$ to approximate the exact inverse $A_{ff}^{-1}:X_f^*\to X_f$. It defines $\widetilde A_{cc}:=A_{cc}-A_{cf}TA_{fc}$, $\widetilde F_c:=F_c-A_{cf}TF_f$, and the modeled fine component $\widetilde u_f:=T r_f(\widetilde u_c)$, where $\widetilde u_c$ solves $\widetilde A_{cc}\widetilde u_c=\widetilde F_c$. This is a finite-dimensional algebraic closure; an application to a PDE requires its own residual, spaces, invertibility, and approximation-defect analysis.

derivations.claim: Write the exact Schur operator and load as $S=A_{cc}-A_{cf}GA_{fc}$ and $g=F_c-A_{cf}GF_f$, so $Su_c=g$. Put $\Delta:=T-G$. The approximate quantities satisfy $\widetilde S=S-A_{cf}\Delta A_{fc}$ and $\widetilde g=g-A_{cf}\Delta F_f$.

Since $\widetilde S\widetilde u_c=\widetilde g$, step 1.1 gives $\widetilde S(\widetilde u_c-u_c)=\widetilde g-\widetilde S u_c=-A_{cf}\Delta(F_f-A_{fc}u_c)=-A_{cf}\Delta r_f$. Apply the induced operator norms and multiply by $\|\widetilde S^{-1}\|$ to prove the coarse bound.

The exact fine component is $u_f=G r_f$. The modeled component is $\widetilde u_f=T(r_f-A_{fc}(\widetilde u_c-u_c))$. Subtracting gives $\widetilde u_f-u_f=(T-G)r_f-TA_{fc}(\widetilde u_c-u_c)$. The triangle inequality and operator norms give the stated fine-scale bound.

For $g_0,g_1\in\mathbb R$, let $S_h(g_0,g_1)$ be the finite-dimensional space of continuous functions on $[0,1]$ that are affine on each cell and have endpoint values $g_0,g_1$. Write $V_h=S_h(0,0)$ for the homogeneous test and trial space. “P1” means polynomial degree at most one on each interval.

Let $\epsilon>0$, $b\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}$, and $f\in C([0,1])$. The stationary boundary-value problem is to find $u\in C^2([0,1])$ such that $-\epsilon u''+b u'=f$ on $(0,1)$, with prescribed endpoint values $u(0)=g_0$ and $u(1)=g_1$. Its dimensionless cell Péclet number is $\mathrm{Pe}=|b|h/(2\epsilon)>0$. The stability theorem on this page uses the homogeneous branch $g_0=g_1=0$; the general endpoint notation also permits the boundary-layer example.

Use the uniform mesh, coefficients, and spaces of [[def-supg-one-dimensional-convection-diffusion-model]]. On every cell set
$$\tau=\frac{h}{2|b|}\left(\coth(\mathrm{Pe})-\frac1{\mathrm{Pe}}\right),\qquad \coth s:=\frac{\cosh s}{\sinh s}.$$
For $w\in S_h(g_0,g_1)+C^2([0,1])$ and $v_h\in V_h$, define
$$a_h(w,v_h):=\epsilon\int_0^1w'v_h'\,dx+b\int_0^1w'v_h\,dx+\sum_{K\in\mathcal T_h}\tau\int_K(-\epsilon w''+bw')(bv_h')\,dx,$$
$$F_h(v_h):=\int_0^1fv_h\,dx+\sum_{K\in\mathcal T_h}\tau\int_K f(bv_h')\,dx.$$
Second derivatives are taken classically on each cell. The strong equation residual is $R_K(w):=-\epsilon w''+bw'-f$. For P1 trial functions, $w_h''=0$ on each cell, so the cell term is $\tau\int_K(bw_h')(bv_h')$. On the smooth consistency extension it retains $-\epsilon w''$; thus the full residual pairing is $\tau\int_K(R_K(w)+f)(bv_h')$, while the load contains the matching $f$ term. The SUPG equation is $a_h(w_h,v_h)=F_h(v_h)$ and adds the same residual-weighted streamline test perturbation to the differential equation and its load.

derivations.claim: Put $q(s)=s\cosh s-\sinh s$. Then $q(0)=0$ and $q'(s)=s\sinh s>0$ for $s>0$, so $q(s)>0$ and $m(s)=q(s)/(s\sinh s)>0$.
The identity $\coth s-1=2/(e^{2s}-1)$ and $e^{2s}-1=\int_0^{2s}e^t\,dt>2s$ give $m(s)<1$.

For $0<s\le1$, $q(s)=\int_0^s t\sinh t\,dt\ge s^3/3$. The function $\sinh s/s$ is increasing because its derivative is $q(s)/s^2>0$, hence $\sinh s\le s\sinh 1$ on this range. Therefore $m(s)\ge s/(3\sinh1)$. For every $s>0$, monotonicity of $\sinh$ also gives $q(s)\le\sinh(s)\int_0^s t\,dt=s^2\sinh(s)/2$, whence $m(s)\le s/2$.

Since $\sinh s>s$ for $s>0$, $m'(s)=s^{-2}-(\sinh s)^{-2}>0$. Thus for $s\ge1$, $m(s)\ge m(1)=\coth1-1$. Together with step 2.2 this proves the two-sided bound. Substituting $s=\mathrm{Pe}$ into [F2] gives the stated lower and first upper bounds on $\tau$, using $h(2|b|)^{-1}\min\{\mathrm{Pe},1\}=\frac12\min\{h^2/(2\epsilon),h/|b|\}$. The last upper bound follows from $m(\mathrm{Pe})\le\mathrm{Pe}/2$.

Fix an integer $N\ge1$, put $h=1/N$, and let $x_j=jh$ for $j=0,\ldots,N$. The cells are $K_j=[x_{j-1},x_j]$. For $g_0,g_1\in\mathbb R$, let $S_h(g_0,g_1)$ be the finite-dimensional space of continuous functions on $[0,1]$ that are affine on each cell and have endpoint values $g_0,g_1$. Write $V_h=S_h(0,0)$ for the homogeneous test and trial space. “P1” means polynomial degree at most one on each interval.

Let $\epsilon>0$, $b\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}$, and $f\in C([0,1])$. The stationary boundary-value problem is to find $u\in C^2([0,1])$ such that $-\epsilon u''+b u'=f$ on $(0,1)$, with prescribed endpoint values $u(0)=g_0$ and $u(1)=g_1$. Its dimensionless cell Péclet number is $\mathrm{Pe}=|b|h/(2\epsilon)>0$. The stability theorem on this page uses the homogeneous branch $g_0=g_1=0$; the general endpoint notation also permits the boundary-layer example.

Use the uniform mesh, coefficients, and spaces of [[def-supg-one-dimensional-convection-diffusion-model]]. On every cell set
$$\tau=\frac{h}{2|b|}\left(\coth(\mathrm{Pe})-\frac1{\mathrm{Pe}}\right),\qquad \coth s:=\frac{\cosh s}{\sinh s}.$$
For $w\in S_h(g_0,g_1)+C^2([0,1])$ and $v_h\in V_h$, define
$$a_h(w,v_h):=\epsilon\int_0^1w'v_h'\,dx+b\int_0^1w'v_h\,dx+\sum_{K\in\mathcal T_h}\tau\int_K(-\epsilon w''+bw')(bv_h')\,dx,$$
$$F_h(v_h):=\int_0^1fv_h\,dx+\sum_{K\in\mathcal T_h}\tau\int_K f(bv_h')\,dx.$$
Second derivatives are taken classically on each cell. The strong equation residual is $R_K(w):=-\epsilon w''+bw'-f$. For P1 trial functions, $w_h''=0$ on each cell, so the cell term is $\tau\int_K(bw_h')(bv_h')$. On the smooth consistency extension it retains $-\epsilon w''$; thus the full residual pairing is $\tau\int_K(R_K(w)+f)(bv_h')$, while the load contains the matching $f$ term. The SUPG equation is $a_h(w_h,v_h)=F_h(v_h)$ and adds the same residual-weighted streamline test perturbation to the differential equation and its load.

Let $s>0$ and define $m(s):=\coth s-1/s$ and $c_*:=\min\{(3\sinh 1)^{-1},\coth 1-1\}>0$. Then
$$c_*\min\{s,1\}\le m(s)<1,\qquad m(s)\le s/2.$$
Consequently, for the parameter in [[def-supg-one-dimensional-residual-form]],
$$0<\frac{c_*}{2}\min\left\{\frac{h^2}{2\epsilon},\frac{h}{|b|}\right\}\le\tau<\frac{h}{2|b|},\qquad \tau\le\frac{h^2}{8\epsilon}.$$

Integration by parts, with $v_h(0)=v_h(1)=0$, gives $\epsilon(u',v_h')+(bu',v_h)=(-\epsilon u''+bu',v_h)=(f,v_h)$. The stabilization contribution to $a_h(u,v_h)$ is $\sum_K\tau(-\epsilon u''+bu',bv_h')_K$, which equals $\sum_K\tau(f,bv_h')_K$ by the strong equation. This is exactly the stabilization contribution to $F_h$, so $a_h(u,v_h)=F_h(v_h)$.

Substituting step 1.1 into [F2] with $w_h=v_h$ yields the displayed identity. Its right side is nonnegative by [F3] and $\epsilon>0$. If it is zero, then $v_h'=0$ on every cell; continuity makes $v_h$ constant on $[0,1]$, and its zero endpoints force $v_h=0$. Hence this quadratic form is a norm squared.

In a basis of the finite-dimensional space $V_h$, the discrete form defines a square linear map $V_h\to V_h^*$. If a vector is in its kernel, testing with that vector and using step 2.1 gives that it is zero. Thus the map is injective, hence bijective in finite equal dimensions, so each discrete load has exactly one solution.
Subtracting the discrete equation from the consistency identity in step 1.2 gives $a_h(u-u_h,v_h)=0$ for every $v_h\in V_h$; the solution exists by step 3.1.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by

By [F2], $a_h(e_h,e_h)=a_h(\eta,e_h)$. The convection term satisfies $(b\eta',e_h)=-(b\eta,e_h')$: cell boundary terms cancel at interior nodes because $\eta$ and $e_h$ are continuous, and the two outer terms vanish. The diffusion and P1 stabilization terms are bounded by $\sqrt{\epsilon}\|\eta'\|_2\|e_h\|_{\mathrm{SD}}$ and $|b|\sqrt{\tau}\|\eta'\|_2\|e_h\|_{\mathrm{SD}}$. The additional consistency-extension term involving $-\epsilon\eta''$ is bounded by $\epsilon\sqrt{\tau}\|\eta''\|_2\|e_h\|_{\mathrm{SD}}$, because $\sqrt{\tau}|b|\|e_h'\|_2\le\|e_h\|_{\mathrm{SD}}$. The integrated convection term is bounded by $\|\eta\|_2\|e_h\|_{\mathrm{SD}}/\sqrt{\tau}$, since $\sqrt{\tau}|b|\|e_h'\|_2\le\|e_h\|_{\mathrm{SD}}$. Therefore $|a_h(\eta,e_h)|\le\left(\sqrt{\epsilon}\|\eta'\|_2+|b|\sqrt{\tau}\|\eta'\|_2+\epsilon\sqrt{\tau}\|\eta''\|_2+\frac{\|\eta\|_2}{\sqrt{\tau}}\right)\|e_h\|_{\mathrm{SD}}$.

If $e_h=0$, its norm estimate is immediate. Otherwise, divide step 2.1 by $\|e_h\|_{\mathrm{SD}}$ and use [F2] to get $\|e_h\|_{\mathrm{SD}}\le(\sqrt{\epsilon}+|b|\sqrt{\tau})\|\eta'\|_2+\epsilon\sqrt{\tau}\|\eta''\|_2+\|\eta\|_2/\sqrt{\tau}$.

Since $I_hu$ is affine on each cell, $\eta''=u''$ cellwise and $\|\eta''\|_2\le M$. With $u-u_h=\eta-e_h$, the triangle inequality, [F1], [F3], [F4], and step 3.1 give $\|u-u_h\|_{\mathrm{SD}}\le\left[h\sqrt{\epsilon+\tau b^2}+h\sqrt{\epsilon}+h|b|\sqrt{\tau}+\epsilon\sqrt{\tau}+\frac{h^2}{\sqrt{\tau}}\right]M$.

From [F5], $h|b|\sqrt{\tau}\le h^{3/2}\sqrt{|b|/2}$. If $\mathrm{Pe}\le1$, then $\tau\ge c_*h^2/(4\epsilon)$, so $h^2/\sqrt{\tau}\le2c_*^{-1/2}h\sqrt{\epsilon}$, and $\epsilon\sqrt{\tau}\le h\sqrt{\epsilon}/\sqrt8$. If $\mathrm{Pe}\ge1$, then $\tau\ge c_*h/(2|b|)$, so $h^2/\sqrt{\tau}\le(2/c_*)^{1/2}h^{3/2}\sqrt{|b|}$; also $\epsilon\le |b|h/2$ and $\tau<h/(2|b|)$ imply $\epsilon\sqrt{\tau}\le h^{3/2}\sqrt{|b|}/(2\sqrt2)$. Finally $h\sqrt{\epsilon+\tau b^2}\le h\sqrt{\epsilon}+h|b|\sqrt{\tau}$. These inequalities prove the second estimate with a universal constant depending only on $c_*$.

Let $X_c$ and $X_f$ be finite-dimensional real vector spaces and set $X=X_c\oplus X_f$; elements are written $(u_c,u_f)$, with $u_c$ the resolved component and $u_f$ the unresolved component. For a real vector space $Y$, let $Y^*$ be its space of real linear functionals. Let $A_{cc}:X_c\to X_c^*$, $A_{cf}:X_f\to X_c^*$, $A_{fc}:X_c\to X_f^*$, and $A_{ff}:X_f\to X_f^*$ be linear maps, with $A_{ff}$ invertible, and let $F_c\in X_c^*$ and $F_f\in X_f^*$. The linear equation on $X$ has block form
$$\begin{pmatrix}A_{cc}&A_{cf}\\A_{fc}&A_{ff}\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}u_c\\u_f\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}F_c\\F_f\end{pmatrix}.$$
The fine residual for a resolved vector $v_c$ is $r_f(v_c):=F_f-A_{fc}v_c$. Exact elimination gives $u_f=A_{ff}^{-1}r_f(u_c)$ and the Schur equation
$$\left(A_{cc}-A_{cf}A_{ff}^{-1}A_{fc}\right)u_c=F_c-A_{cf}A_{ff}^{-1}F_f.$$

A **residual closure** selects a linear map $T:X_f^*\to X_f$ to approximate the exact inverse $A_{ff}^{-1}:X_f^*\to X_f$. It defines $\widetilde A_{cc}:=A_{cc}-A_{cf}TA_{fc}$, $\widetilde F_c:=F_c-A_{cf}TF_f$, and the modeled fine component $\widetilde u_f:=T r_f(\widetilde u_c)$, where $\widetilde u_c$ solves $\widetilde A_{cc}\widetilde u_c=\widetilde F_c$. This is a finite-dimensional algebraic closure; an application to a PDE requires its own residual, spaces, invertibility, and approximation-defect analysis.

Use the block operators and residual closure of [[def-supg-variational-multiscale-block-closure]]. Equip $X_c,X_f$ and their duals with norms, and use the corresponding induced operator norms. Let $G:=A_{ff}^{-1}$, assume the exact Schur system has a solution $u_c$, and put $r_f:=F_f-A_{fc}u_c$. Suppose the closure map $T$ has $\widetilde S:=A_{cc}-A_{cf}TA_{fc}$ invertible, and let $\widetilde u_c$ solve the approximate Schur system. Then
$$\|\widetilde u_c-u_c\|\le\|\widetilde S^{-1}\|\,\|A_{cf}\|\,\|T-G\|\,\|r_f\|,$$
and for the modeled fine component $\widetilde u_f=T(F_f-A_{fc}\widetilde u_c)$,
$$\|\widetilde u_f-u_f\|\le\|T-G\|\,\|r_f\|+\|T\|\,\|A_{fc}\|\,\|\widetilde u_c-u_c\|.$$
The exact fine scale is $u_f=G r_f$. These bounds concern finite-dimensional algebraic blocks; they do not certify a universal PDE subgrid model.

Let $\epsilon>0$, $b\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}$, and $f\in C([0,1])$. The stationary boundary-value problem is to find $u\in C^2([0,1])$ such that $-\epsilon u''+b u'=f$ on $(0,1)$, with prescribed endpoint values $u(0)=g_0$ and $u(1)=g_1$. Its dimensionless cell Péclet number is $\mathrm{Pe}=|b|h/(2\epsilon)>0$. The stability theorem on this page uses the homogeneous branch $g_0=g_1=0$; the general endpoint notation also permits the boundary-layer example.

Use the uniform mesh, coefficients, and spaces of [[def-supg-one-dimensional-convection-diffusion-model]]. On every cell set
$$\tau=\frac{h}{2|b|}\left(\coth(\mathrm{Pe})-\frac1{\mathrm{Pe}}\right),\qquad \coth s:=\frac{\cosh s}{\sinh s}.$$
For $w\in S_h(g_0,g_1)+C^2([0,1])$ and $v_h\in V_h$, define
$$a_h(w,v_h):=\epsilon\int_0^1w'v_h'\,dx+b\int_0^1w'v_h\,dx+\sum_{K\in\mathcal T_h}\tau\int_K(-\epsilon w''+bw')(bv_h')\,dx,$$

For P1 trial functions, $w_h''=0$ on each cell, so the cell term is $\tau\int_K(bw_h')(bv_h')$. On the smooth consistency extension it retains $-\epsilon w''$; thus the full residual pairing is $\tau\int_K(R_K(w)+f)(bv_h')$, while the load contains the matching $f$ term. The SUPG equation is $a_h(w_h,v_h)=F_h(v_h)$ and adds the same residual-weighted streamline test perturbation to the differential equation and its load.

Let $s>0$ and define $m(s):=\coth s-1/s$ and $c_*:=\min\{(3\sinh 1)^{-1},\coth 1-1\}>0$. Then
$$c_*\min\{s,1\}\le m(s)<1,\qquad m(s)\le s/2.$$

$$0<\frac{c_*}{2}\min\left\{\frac{h^2}{2\epsilon},\frac{h}{|b|}\right\}\le\tau<\frac{h}{2|b|},\qquad \tau\le\frac{h^2}{8\epsilon}.$$

citations.quote:
Fix an integer $N\ge1$, put $h=1/N$, and let $x_j=jh$ for $j=0,\ldots,N$. The cells are $K_j=[x_{j-1},x_j]$. For $g_0,g_1\in\mathbb R$, let $S_h(g_0,g_1)$ be the finite-dimensional space of continuous functions on $[0,1]$ that are affine on each cell and have endpoint values $g_0,g_1$. Write $V_h=S_h(0,0)$ for the homogeneous test and trial space. “P1” means polynomial degree at most one on each interval.

Let $\epsilon>0$, $b\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}$, and $f\in C([0,1])$. The stationary boundary-value problem is to find $u\in C^2([0,1])$ such that $-\epsilon u''+b u'=f$ on $(0,1)$, with prescribed endpoint values $u(0)=g_0$ and $u(1)=g_1$. Its dimensionless cell Péclet number is $\mathrm{Pe}=|b|h/(2\epsilon)>0$. The stability theorem on this page uses the homogeneous branch $g_0=g_1=0$; the general endpoint notation also permits the boundary-layer example.

Use the uniform mesh, coefficients, and spaces of [[def-supg-one-dimensional-convection-diffusion-model]]. On every cell set
$$\tau=\frac{h}{2|b|}\left(\coth(\mathrm{Pe})-\frac1{\mathrm{Pe}}\right),\qquad \coth s:=\frac{\cosh s}{\sinh s}.$$
For $w\in S_h(g_0,g_1)+C^2([0,1])$ and $v_h\in V_h$, define
$$a_h(w,v_h):=\epsilon\int_0^1w'v_h'\,dx+b\int_0^1w'v_h\,dx+\sum_{K\in\mathcal T_h}\tau\int_K(-\epsilon w''+bw')(bv_h')\,dx,$$
$$F_h(v_h):=\int_0^1fv_h\,dx+\sum_{K\in\mathcal T_h}\tau\int_K f(bv_h')\,dx.$$
Second derivatives are taken classically on each cell. The strong equation residual is $R_K(w):=-\epsilon w''+bw'-f$. For P1 trial functions, $w_h''=0$ on each cell, so the cell term is $\tau\int_K(bw_h')(bv_h')$. On the smooth consistency extension it retains $-\epsilon w''$; thus the full residual pairing is $\tau\int_K(R_K(w)+f)(bv_h')$, while the load contains the matching $f$ term. The SUPG equation is $a_h(w_h,v_h)=F_h(v_h)$ and adds the same residual-weighted streamline test perturbation to the differential equation and its load.

Let $s>0$ and define $m(s):=\coth s-1/s$ and $c_*:=\min\{(3\sinh 1)^{-1},\coth 1-1\}>0$. Then
$$c_*\min\{s,1\}\le m(s)<1,\qquad m(s)\le s/2.$$
Consequently, for the parameter in [[def-supg-one-dimensional-residual-form]],
$$0<\frac{c_*}{2}\min\left\{\frac{h^2}{2\epsilon},\frac{h}{|b|}\right\}\le\tau<\frac{h}{2|b|},\qquad \tau\le\frac{h^2}{8\epsilon}.$$

derivations.claim: Put $r=b/\epsilon$. The function $u(x)=(e^{rx}-1)/(e^r-1)$ has endpoint values $0,1$, and $-\epsilon u''+bu'=(-\epsilon r^2+br)e^{rx}/(e^r-1)=0$. Hence it is the exact solution.

Let $\phi$ be the P1 hat function at $x=h=1/2$, let $\chi_h\in S_h(0,1)$ have nodal values $(0,0,1)$, and write $u_h=U\phi+\chi_h$. Put $D=\epsilon+\tau b^2$. Since $\phi'=1/h$ on the left cell and $-1/h$ on the right, $\int_0^1(\phi')^2dx=2/h$ and $\int_0^1\phi'\phi\,dx=\frac12[\phi^2]_0^1=0$, so $a_h(\phi,\phi)=2D/h$. Also $\chi_h'=0$ on the left and $1/h$ on the right, giving $D\int\chi_h'\phi'=-D/h$ and $b\int\chi_h'\phi=b/h\int_h^1\phi=b/2$. Thus $a_h(\chi_h,\phi)=-D/h+b/2$ and the one interior equation is $D(2U-1)/h+b/2=0$. By [F3], $D=\epsilon+(bh/2)(\coth(\mathrm{Pe})-1/\mathrm{Pe})=(bh/2)\coth(\mathrm{Pe})$, so $U=(1-\tanh(\mathrm{Pe}))/2=1/(e^{2\mathrm{Pe}}+1)$. The exact value $u(h)=(e^{bh/\epsilon}-1)/(e^{2bh/\epsilon}-1)$ is the same number because $2\mathrm{Pe}=bh/\epsilon$.

At $x=0.99$, the piecewise-linear value is $u_h(0.99)=0.98+0.02U$, which tends to $0.98$ as $\epsilon\downarrow0$. The exact value is $(e^{0.99b/\epsilon}-1)/(e^{b/\epsilon}-1)$, which tends to zero because $b>0$ and $0.99<1$. Therefore the pointwise error tends to $0.98$. The exact midpoint node does not resolve the exponential layer inside the final cell.
